EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Precipitation associated with an intensifying low pressure system over the Deep South developed along the I-40 corridor in the North Carolina foothills and Piedmont during the afternoon of the 24th, beginning as a mix of snow and sleet. The precip quickly transitioned to mostly sleet, which continued into the overnight and early morning of the 25th. The sleet began to mix with freezing rain after sunrise on the 25th, briefly becoming all sleet before ending early in the evening. Total sleet accumulations of 1 to 2 inches occurred, with up to 3 inches reported across Davie County. Ice accretion was Generally around 0.1 inch, with amounts up to 0.25 inch reported closer to the Blue Ridge escarpment.

Severe Drought conditions were introduced across the North Carolina and Virginia Piedmonts in early January after the previous two months of November and December recorded precipitation totals of 2.00-4.00 inches, which ended up being 25 to 50 percent of normal for that period. These dry conditions combined with the dry fall conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November and December, contributed to a rapid decrease in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd to 5th percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 6th of January. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the Yadkin River, which was observed to be below the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

Arctic high pressure arrived by January 27 in the wake of a departing winter storm. However, the pressure gradient between the high arriving and the low departing provided gusty winds that combined with the cold air to provide dangerously low wind chills. Wind chills dropped below -15��F during the late evening hours of January 26 into the early morning hours of January 27 in Ashe and Watauga counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several mesonet weather stations reported wind chill values dropping to -15��F or lower. The lowest wind chill value recorded was -28��F at Mount Jefferson.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Precipitation associated with an intensifying low pressure system over the Deep South developed in areas along and near the Blue Ridge escarpment during the late evening of the 24th, beginning mainly as sleet. The sleet, occasionally mixed with snow continued into the early morning of the 25th, when it began to mix with and eventually change to freezing rain. The freezing rain was mostly light until a band of heavy freezing rain moved over the area late in the afternoon. Total sleet accumulations of 1 to 2 inches occurred, with around 0.5 inch (locally as high as 0.75 inch) ice accretion on top of the sleet, resulting in very hazardous driving conditions. Unusually cold temperatures following the event resulted in travel difficulties that lingered for several days.

An area of low pressure developed across Texas and moved eastward towards the Appalachian Mountains, while Arctic high pressure also tracked eastward across the northern Plains and Great Lakes. The Arctic high reached the Appalachian Mountains first and wedged southward against the eastern slopes of the Blue Ridge to provide cold air near the surface. Meanwhile, the area of low pressure dissipated across the mountains, while a secondary area of low pressure formed off the North Carolina coast. This pattern set up a Miller B winter storm with the precipitation type as initially snow on January 24 but changing over to sleet and freezing rain by January 25 due to a substantial warm nose aloft. Notable impacts were documented during this winter storm in the form of power outages and transportation delays.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A wintry mix occurred with reports of up to 3.5 inches of snow, up to 2.0 inches of sleet, and up to 0.05 inches of freezing rain. Key Impacts: power outages, transportation delays.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of low pressure developed across Texas and moved eastward towards the Appalachian Mountains, while Arctic high pressure also tracked eastward across the northern Plains and Great Lakes. The Arctic high reached the Appalachian Mountains first and wedged southward against the eastern slopes of the Blue Ridge to provide cold air near the surface. Meanwhile, the area of low pressure dissipated across the mountains, while a secondary area of low pressure formed off the North Carolina coast. This pattern set up a Miller B winter storm with the precipitation type as initially snow on January 24 but changing over to sleet and freezing rain by January 25 due to a substantial warm nose aloft. Notable impacts were documented during this winter storm in the form of power outages and transportation delays.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A wintry mix occurred with reports of up to 3.1 inches of snow, up to 2.6 inches of sleet, and up to 0.05 inches of freezing rain. Key Impacts: power outages, transportation delays.

Severe Drought conditions were introduced across the North Carolina and Virginia Piedmonts in early January after the previous two months of November and December recorded precipitation totals of 2.00-4.00 inches, which ended up being 25 to 50 percent of normal for that period. These dry conditions combined with the dry fall conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November and December, contributed to a rapid decrease in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd to 5th percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 6th of January. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the Yadkin River, which was observed to be below the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe Drought conditions were introduced to Caswell county in early January after the previous two months of November and December recorded precipitation totals of 2.00-4.00 inches, which ended up being 25 to 50 percent of normal for that period. These dry conditions combined with the dry fall conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November and December,  contributed to a rapid decrease in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 5th percentile for groundwater, and 5th percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 6th of January. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the Dan River, which was observed to be below the 5th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A potent upper-level low tracked south and then southeast from the Upper Midwest to the Southeast during the weekend of Friday January 30th to Sunday February 1st. At the same time, a baroclinic zone set up along the offshore waters of Georgia, westwards to the Deep South. A surface low then developed along this baroclinic zone just off the coast of Georgia during the early morning hours on Saturday. As the upper level low neared the developing surface low, this resulted in a Miller-A low pressure system. The associated offshore low pressure system then rapidly deepened as it tracked northeastwards just off the North Carolina coast during the overnight hours between Saturday and Sunday. This very strong low then pulled away from the Carolinas and moved out into the open waters of the North Atlantic during the late morning hours on Sunday. With an unusually cold airmass in place across the Southeast and Mid-Atlantic, a rather widespread and historic snowstorm for almost all of Eastern North Carolina occurred. Snow began during the morning hours on Saturday mainly along the Crystal Coast and Inner Banks, though a period of light snow occurred across portions of the Coastal Plain as well Saturday morning. By Saturday afternoon the low pressure system off the coast began to deepen quickly resulting in heavier and more widespread snowfall across much of Eastern North Carolina. Snowfall rates became heavy at times resulting in periods of whiteout conditions as 30-50 mph wind gusts (60-65 mph on the Outer Banks) also impacted the area making travel treacherous across the region. Snow finally pushed completely offshore by the late morning hours on Sunday. Over 10 inches of snowfall were measured across most counties of Eastern North Carolina outside of Hatteras Island and Ocracoke with several counties reporting over a foot of snowfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Widespread reports between public, CoCoRahs, trained spotters, and NWS employees of ten to nineteen inches of snowfall including fifteen inches of snowfall at the NWS Newport Morehead City office. Snowfall occurred between the morning of January thirty-first and the morning of February first.

Increasing southwest winds overnight resulted in steadily warming temperatures allowing the precipitation to change to freezing rain and rain across the Smokies and vicinity by daybreak. By mid-morning, precip had changed to rain across the entire area. Total sleet and snow accumulations generally ranged from one tenth to around one half inch. Some high elevation locations as well as some locations in the upper Tuckasegee and upper Pigeon valleys also saw a few hundredths of an inch of ice accretion.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A powerful winter storm developed on 24 January and did not fully let up until early on 26 January. After a strong Arctic cold front arrived the prior day, an area of low pressure tracked across the southeastern United States, bringing a plume of moisture into the Carolinas. A wintry mix of freezing rain, sleet, and snow developed, with the greatest snow and sleet accumulations over the Piedmont and the highest ice accumulations over the Sandhills and Coastal Plain of central North Carolina.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Around an inch of snow and sleet fell, along with trace amounts of freezing rain.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Precipitation associated with an intensifying low pressure system over the Deep South developed across the southern North Carolina foothills around midnight early on the 25th. The precipitation began as mostly sleet, which continued through the early morning hours before mixing with, and eventually changing to freezing rain later in the morning. The precipitation finally tapered off during the early evening. Total sleet accumulations of 1 to 2 inches occurred, with around 0.25 inch of ice accreting on top of the sleet. This made for very hazardous driving conditions. Due to unusually cold weather following the event, several days of refreezing resulted in travel difficulties continuing during the overnight and morning hours.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure area with a cold front attached to it tracked east across the Carolinas during the late morning and afternoon timeframe. Along and and out ahead of the cold front a line of scattered to numerous severe thunderstorms developed and quickly raced east northeast across Eastern NC, producing 60 to 70 mph wind gusts. With ample instability and strong wind shear in place several of the storms interacted with the sea breeze inland from the coast and produced several tornadoes, in addition to severe thunderstorm wind damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large tree was blown down on John Small Ave/US Highway 264.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Plummeting snow levels in the wake of a cold front interacted with strong northwest upslope flow to result in snow shower development beginning during the afternoon of the 16th across the counties bordering Tennesse. The snow showers continued through the overnight hours before beginning to wind down during the morning of the 17th, before tapering off during the afternoon. Total accumulations of 3-6 inches, with locally higher amounts were reported in the higher elevations along the Tennessee border. Accumulations up to 3 inches occurred in the valleys northeast of I-40, while valley locations beneath the Smokies saw little more than a dusting.

A line of showers and thunderstorms, with embedded strong-to-severe storms moved across western North Carolina through the morning into the early afternoon. Several isolated, weak tornadoes occurred, along with sporadic pockets of damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A brief, weak tornado with touched down just south of Mars Hill between Interstate-26 and South Main St. It traveled for about half a mile, uprooting several trees and snapping branches before lifting near Bold Springs Dr.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of showers and thunderstorms, with embedded strong-to-severe storms moved across western North Carolina through the morning into the early afternoon. Several isolated, weak tornadoes occurred, along with sporadic pockets of damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A weak tornado touched down along N Graham St near the intersection of Moretz Ave, where several small trees were snapped. The tornado moved northeast into a residential area, where additional large limbs were snapped. The tornado reached peak intensity of 85 mph as it crossed Atando Ave where sheet metal was peeled back off a large industrial building. Another warehouse sustained more significant roof damage with a large section of roofing removed. Several large pine trees were snapped behind the warehouse. The tornado weakened and eventually dissipated as it moved into another residential area along Drury Dr where a few small limbs were downed.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An approaching cold front, supported by an upper-level shortwave trough, triggered widely scattered thunderstorms. Decreasing cloud cover during late afternoon allowed instability to increase, with CAPE values in Blacksburg, VA reaching as high as 3,000 J/Kg per the 30/00z upper air sounding. Lapse rates were observed near 7 C/km, while 0-1km shear was observed at around 40 knots. Storms developed along the Blue Ridge and pushed east into the Piedmont, increasing in intensity across the southern Piedmont. Storms then congealed into a broken line that tracked southeast. Although no hail was reported, there were several reports of trees blown down by thunderstorm winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail of three quarter inch in diameter was reported near Reese, NC.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A few thunderstorms moved through Eastern NC during the later evening hours of April 5th. One particular storm became severe and produced damaging straight line winds of up to 80-90 mph.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: In coordination with Pamlico County Emergency Management, a survey of damage along HWY 55 in Stonewall found damage consistent with straight line winds of 80 to 90 mph. In this area, a mobile home strapped down with hurricane ties was moved 3 to 4 feet off its foundation. The ties were ripped out of the ground. The home sustained damage to siding and windows. An occupant inside the home during the storm sustained injuries. The home was blown off the foundation towards the east. A nearby home on Spain Farm Road sustained minor damage to a patio and outdoor light fixtures. The time was estimated based on observer report and radar.

Extreme Drought conditions were introduced across north central and northwest North Carolina in early and late April after the previous several months of January, February, and March recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, with locally lower totals of 4.00-6.00 inches. This ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period, with locally lower percentiles in the 25 to 50 percent of normal. These continued dry conditions combined with the dry fall and early winter conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, January, February, and March contributed to a continued decline in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 21th of April. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the Yadkin, New, and Dan River basins, which were all observed to be around the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows. A couple snowfall events in late February contributed to some relief in streamflows and areawide drought conditions; however, precipitation totals still fell short, and overall lead to some minor Severe Drought Expansions across the area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A potent upper-level low tracked south and then southeast from the Upper Midwest to the Southeast during the weekend of Friday January 30th to Sunday February 1st. At the same time, a baroclinic zone set up along the offshore waters of Georgia, westwards to the Deep South. A surface low then developed along this baroclinic zone just off the coast of Georgia during the early morning hours on Saturday January 31st. As the upper level low neared the developing surface low, this resulted in a Miller-A low pressure system. The associated offshore low pressure system then rapidly strengthened as it tracked northeastwards just off the North Carolina coast during the overnight hours between Saturday and Sunday. This very strong low then pulled away from the Carolinas and moved out into the open waters of the North Atlantic during the late morning hours on Sunday. With an unusually cold airmass in place across the Southeast and Mid-Atlantic, a rather widespread and historic snowstorm for almost all of Eastern North Carolina occurred. Snow began during the morning hours on Saturday January 31st mainly along the Crystal Coast and Inner Banks, though a period of light snow occurred across portions of the Coastal Plain as well Saturday morning. By Saturday afternoon the low pressure system off the coast began to deepen quickly resulting in heavier and more widespread snowfall across much of Eastern North Carolina. Snowfall rates became heavy at times resulting in periods of whiteout conditions as 30-50 mph wind gusts (60-65 mph on the Outer Banks) also impacted the area making travel treacherous across the region. Snow finally pushed completely offshore by the late morning hours on Sunday February 1st. Over 10 inches of snowfall were measured across most counties of Eastern North Carolina outside of Hatteras Island and Ocracoke with several counties reporting over a foot of snowfall. The strong winds associated with the low also produced coastal flooding on the Outer Banks of Hatteras and Ocracoke Islands. Highway 12 was closed for a time, and 4 more homes in the Buxton area collapsed into the ocean due to the coastal flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An NWS employee reported snowfall totals of sixteen inches near Hubert, North Carolina, with several additional reports from the public and CoCoRaHS stations reporting between twelve and seventeen inches of snowfall across Onslow County. Snowfall fell between the morning hours on January thirty-first and the morning of February first.

By Saturday afternoon the low pressure system off the coast began to deepen quickly resulting in heavier and more widespread snowfall across much of Eastern North Carolina. Snowfall rates became heavy at times resulting in periods of whiteout conditions as 30-50 mph wind gusts (60-65 mph on the Outer Banks) also impacted the area making travel treacherous across the region. Snow finally pushed completely offshore by the late morning hours on Sunday February 1st. Over 10 inches of snowfall were measured across most counties of Eastern North Carolina outside of Hatteras Island and Ocracoke with several counties reporting over a foot of snowfall. The strong winds associated with the low also produced coastal flooding on the Outer Banks of Hatteras and Ocracoke Islands. Highway 12 was closed for a time, and 4 more homes in the Buxton area collapsed into the ocean due to the coastal flooding.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme Drought conditions were introduced across north central and northwest North Carolina in early and late April after the previous several months of January, February, and March recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, with locally lower totals of 4.00-6.00 inches. This ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period, with locally lower percentiles in the 25 to 50 percent of normal. These continued dry conditions combined with the dry fall and early winter conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, January, February, and March contributed to a continued decline in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 21th of April. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the Yadkin, New, and Dan River basins, which were all observed to be around the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows. A couple snowfall events in late February contributed to some relief in streamflows and areawide drought conditions; however, precipitation totals still fell short, and overall lead to some minor Severe Drought Expansions across the area.

Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the Dan River, which was observed to be below the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: After a near-record dry April, the impacts of months-long precipitation deficits as high as 18 resulted in extreme to exceptional drought conditions lingering into May across western North Carolina. Many pastures and hayfields were rated poor-to-very poor, resulting in forage shortages. Crop stress affected soybeans, delayed or reduced planting for corn and other crops, and lowered vegetable yields. Reservoirs, lakes, and streams were well below normal (e.g. Fontana Lake around 18 feet below normal). Mandatory or voluntary conservation measures were in place in multiple systems, and  some ponds and smaller supplies were critically low. Fire danger remained abnormally high and the wildfire season extended into May across the mountains, although the threat steadily decreased during the first half of the month owing to greenup and a continued statewide burn ban. A transition to a very wet pattern finally brought some relief late in the month, especially to the Blue Ridge, the foothills, and the southern Piedmont, where May rainfall wound up 125 to 175% of normal. Drought category was reduced to severe across much of these areas by the start of June.

Multiple thunderstorms developed during the afternoon and evening of the May 27th across northwest North Carolina as a strong upper level disturbance passed across the lower Mid-Atlantic along a stationary front draped across the region. The storms developed in a moderately unstable environment, with surface temperatures observed in the low to mid 80s during the afternoon, while dewpoints were observed in the upper 60s to low 70s. This helped to drive MLCAPE values into the 1,500 to 2,000 J/kg range, with relatively steep low-level lapse rates. Area wind profilers also indicated westerly winds within the low levels of the atmosphere, with 30-35 kt of deep-layer shear supporting damaging wind gusts in the stronger thunderstorm activity.

Extreme Drought conditions remained across north central North Carolina, and Exceptional Drought conditions expanded into northwest North Carolina in early and late May after the previous several months of February, March, and April recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, with locally lower totals of 4.00-6.00 inches. This ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period, with locally lower percentiles in the 25 to 50 percent of normal. These continued dry conditions combined with the dry fall and early winter conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, January, February, March, and April contributed to a continued decline in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 1st of May. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the Yadkin, New, and Dan River basins, which were all observed to be around the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous showers and thunderstorms developed across western North Carolina during the afternoon and evening. A series of thunderstorm cells became anchored on the slopes of Bearwallow Mountain in Henderson County, resulting in torrential rainfall that lasted for a couple of hours, resulting in flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple sources reported significant flash flooding developed across northeast Henderson County after 4 to 7 inches of rain fell on the slopes of Bearwallow Mountain in just a couple of hours. The main impact was to Clear Creek and its tributaries, including Puncheon Camp Creek, Cox Creek, and Laurel Fork. A culvert washed out underneath a section of Highway 74 in the Gerton community, forcing closure of the road for a few days. A section of Bearwallow Rd was also washed out in the Edneyville area. Multiple other roads were inundated and closed throughout the area, while multiple culverts under private driveways and some small bridges were reportedly washed out or damaged. A few homes were briefly isolated due to washed out culverts or flooded roads. The high flows on Clear Creek, combined with subsequent heavy rainfall in the Mud Creek basin resulted in the French Broad River rising to bankfull in Flecther and vicinity.

Strong northwest winds pushing colder air into the area in the wake of an arctic cold front interacting with moisture banked against the western slopes of the Appalachians resulted in a protracted period of snow showers developing near the Tennessee/North Carolina border. The snow showers began developing on the morning of the 22nd, and continued off and on for more than 36 hours before tapering off during the early morning of the 24th. Snowfall totals were heavily dependent upon elevation and exposure to northwest winds, with accumulations of 8-12 inches reported above 3500 feet across Avery County. Totals in the lower elevations were more in the 3 to 6 inch range.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Very strong-to-damaging wind gusts from the northwest developed during the morning across the mountains near the Blue Ridge escarpment in the wake of a cold front. Frequent gusts of 50-60 mph, with occasional gusts as high as 65 mph occurred in the lower elevations. Meanwhile, winds gusted as high as 80 mph on exposed peaks and ridgetops. Numerous trees and large tree limbs were blown down throughout the area, with some trees falling on power lines and causing scattered power outages.

Life-threatening cold that began during the afternoon of the 31st continued through the morning of the 1st across the North Carolina mountains. Winds gusting in the 35 to 50 mph range combined with air temperatures in the single digits to result in minimum wind chills of -5 to -15 across the valleys. Stronger winds combined with air temperatures from 0 to -10 to result in wind chills of -15 or lower across the high elevations, with some exposed high peaks and ridegetops reporting values as low as -35.
